newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt polling now behind election support.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt polling now behind election support.

text.p: We reached a turning point in the history of the Liberal-National government this month: its opinion-poll standing slipped below the election level.
Reuters Poll Trend estimates of the two-party preferred vote show that if an election were held in mid-February the government probably would have lost seats.
The government's trend two-party lead was 6.7 percent points (call it "probably less than seven"), compared with the March 2 gap of 7.2 points, according to the poll trend issued on Friday.
The government would still have won the election, of course. The Liberal-Nationals are still ahead of Labor.
But the news is that the easy days are over.
Unpopular government decisions may no longer simply burn part of an enormous stock of political capital, such as the 14-point lead the administration enjoyed in early November.
Now an unpopular decision may mean the loss of more backbench members of parliament in marginal seats.
The current two-party gap certainly does not show a government in trouble. But it might prompt a government to be cautious.
Some of the government's critics assert that it is a timid, poll-driven administration.
Canberra Watch feels the evidence on this is inconclusive.

Certainly, the coalition parties have been unadventurous for conservatives kept out of government for 13 years, but note that Prime Minister John Howard had good reasons to define a limited programme of reform before the election.
He remembered what had happened to John Hewson's bold plans.
But let's assume for the moment that the critics are right and that Howard checks his polls before making a decision. If so, we can expect little adventurous reform between now and the next election.
The party room will have perhaps a more powerful effect, because the Liberal-Nationals have a swarm of backbenchers on marginal seats -- the seats that used to be safe Labor ones.
If the polls solidify with a lead below that enjoyed at election time, terrified marginal backbenchers will continuously lobby Howard to play it safe.
Poll analysis needs a few cautions, however.

Firstly, the Reuters Poll Trend, as a moving average of the three big polls, is subject to revision. The 6.7-point gap estimated for February 16 might be revised up a little. On the other hand, it might go down.

Secondly, there is no great precision in these numbers. Canberra Watch is confident that the trend number is a more useful guide than the very volatile three-poll average (which, incidentally, showed a 6.5 point gap in mid Februrary) but a margin for error of at least one percentage point must be allowed.
And finally, the two-party number is itself quite volatile -- so volatile that most analysis focuses on the primary vote.

The difference between the two measures is so-called preference votes -- minor party support that is redistributed to the two big blocs in each House of Representatives ballot in accordance with each voter's numbered preference.

An examination of the Reuters Poll Trend series suggests that either the polls have some special difficulty detecting the two-party vote or, more likely, minor party voters simply switch their preference between the big blocs quite readily.
In fact, it seems that they tend to slosh backwards and forwards with the big-party supporters, greatly magnifying any rise or fall in government support.
Minor-party voters seem to be something like water inside a boat. If something makes the boat list, the water runs across to that side and makes it list more.
All of this means: be careful in making assumptions about polls and particularly about two-party support.
Still, such uncertainty flows both ways and might only make the government more cautious still.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
